title: The lonely school: Quote, effect, So What (A Christmas Carol)
sub: Last week you got every analysis question right on the empty town. This week the passage is here for you: a real GCSE extract from Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, about a lonely boy in an empty school. About 15 minutes on screen, then two paragraphs on paper.
target: AQA Literature Level 3 needs “explained comments on the writer’s methods” and Level 4 “clear explanation”. Each paragraph: a short quote, the effect of a word or method in it, then So What: what it shows about loneliness.

sections.sub: Last week: the empty town. From memory.

blocks.q: Which sentence analyses rather than retells?
o: Scrooge goes back to his old school with the Ghost.
Dickens makes the school feel cold and forgotten, which suggests that loneliness has shaped Scrooge since he was a child.
There is a boy reading in the school.
blocks.why: Retelling says what happens. Analysis says what the writer makes us feel and what that suggests.

blocks.q: Which is the best quote to analyse?
o: “They went, the Ghost and Scrooge, across the hall, to a door at the back of the house.”
blocks.why: Short quotes let you zoom in on one word. “feeble” is a word you can say a lot about. The long one is mostly plot.

blocks.html:
AQA English Literature 8702/1N, June 2022, extract for Q02 (Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Chapter 2)

In this extract, the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge back to his school.

“The school is not quite deserted,” said the Ghost. “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.”

Scrooge said he knew it. And he sobbed.

They left the high-road, by a well-remembered lane, and soon approached a mansion of dull red brick, with a little weathercock-surmounted cupola, on the roof, and a bell hanging in it. It was a large house, but one of broken fortunes; for the spacious offices were little used, their walls were damp and mossy, their windows broken, and their gates decayed. Fowls clucked and strutted in the stables; and the coach-houses and sheds were over-run with grass. Nor was it more retentive of its ancient state, within; for entering the dreary hall, and glancing through the open doors of many rooms, they found them poorly furnished, cold, and vast. There was an earthy savour in the air, a chilly bareness in the place, which associated itself somehow with too much getting up by candle-light, and not too much to eat.

They went, the Ghost and Scrooge, across the hall, to a door at the back of the house. It opened before them, and disclosed a long, bare, melancholy room, made barer still by lines of plain deal forms and desks. At one of these a lonely boy was reading near a feeble fire; and Scrooge sat down upon a form, and wept to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be.

Not a latent echo in the house, not a squeak and scuffle from the mice behind the panelling, not a drip from the half-thawed water-spout in the dull yard behind, not a sigh among the leafless boughs of one despondent poplar, not the idle swinging of an empty store-house door, no, not a clicking in the fire, but fell upon the heart of Scrooge with a softening influence, and gave a freer passage to his tears.

Words: cupola a small dome; retentive of its ancient state keeping its old grandeur; savour smell or taste; forms wooden benches; deal cheap pine; latent hidden; despondent hopeless, low.

blocks.q: ‘a lonely boy was reading near a feeble fire’. What is the main effect of “feeble”?
o: It tells us the fire was small.
A fire should mean warmth and comfort; a feeble one gives almost none, so even the comfort in the room is weak, like the care the boy gets.
blocks.why: “It is alliteration” names the method but says nothing about the effect (AQA Level 2: identification). “The fire was small” retells. The effect links the word to the boy’s loneliness. (The alliteration of ‘feeble fire’ is in AQA’s own mark scheme: name it, then say what it does.)

blocks.q: ‘a long, bare, melancholy room, made barer still’. How does this work?
o: Three adjectives pile up emptiness and sadness, then “barer still” makes it worse: the room seems to empty itself as we look.
It uses a lot of commas.
blocks.why: Say what the method does: the build-up, then “barer still” going one step further. That is explaining the method, which moves you from Level 2 to Level 3.

blocks.q: ‘Scrooge … wept to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be.’ Which is the strongest So What?
o: This suggests the hard, cold man we met in Chapter 1 was made by loneliness: Dickens wants us to see that Scrooge was once a child nobody cared for, so he can still be changed.
blocks.why: The So What connects the quote to the big idea (loneliness shapes people, and they can change). “Scrooge is sad” is true but stops at the surface.

blocks.q: Four comments on ‘a solitary child, neglected by his friends’. Tap them from weakest to strongest.
items: The Ghost says there is a child left at the school.
Dickens uses the word “solitary”, which is an adjective.
“Solitary” means completely alone, and “neglected” suggests someone should have cared for him but did not.
“Neglected” suggests the child was left alone by others, not by choice, which suggests Dickens blames a lack of care, not the child, for the lonely man Scrooge becomes.
blocks.done: The top comment does all three: quote, effect, So What.

blocks.q: Choose one short quote from the last paragraph (“Not a latent echo… freer passage to his tears”). Write: the quote, the effect of a word or method in it, and So What about loneliness.

points.t: a short, exact quote from the last paragraph
the effect of a word or method (e.g. the repeated “not a…” shows how silent the house is)
a So What about loneliness: what it shows about Scrooge or Dickens’ ideas

mark.note: A hint: count the “not”s. Why might silence make Scrooge cry, rather than a sound?

blocks.html: Print the written paper. It is the real GCSE question. For now, write about the extract only: two or three Quote, effect, So What paragraphs, by hand, in 25 minutes. Then mark it against AQA’s levels on the last page.

items: Every quote is short (a few words) and exact.
After each quote, I explained the effect of one word or method.
Every paragraph ends with So What: what it shows about loneliness.
I named methods only when I also said what they do.
I wrote about Dickens’ choices (“Dickens makes…”), not just Scrooge.

blocks.q: “Why does Dickens show us Scrooge as a lonely boy?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for a So What, e.g. “so we understand how he became cold, and believe he can change”. If she retells (“because the ghost takes him there”), ask “and what does that make us think about Scrooge?”

blocks.h: Plan (5 min): one row per paragraph

blocks.stem: Your version this week: write about the extract only, two or three paragraphs. (The full GCSE answer also covers the novel as a whole.)
blocks.q:
Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents the effects of loneliness and isolation in A Christmas Carol.

Write about:
• how Dickens presents the effects of loneliness and isolation in this extract
• how Dickens presents the effects of loneliness and isolation in the novel as a whole.

selfcheck: Each paragraph has a short, exact quote.
Each paragraph explains the effect of one word or method.
Each paragraph ends with So What: what it shows about loneliness.
I used at least one method name (adjective, list, repetition, contrast) and said what it does.
Reflection: which So What was hardest to write? Where would you put yourself on the levels below?

marking.h: AQA’s levels (8702/1N mark scheme, AO2: the writer’s methods)
marking.html:
• Level 2 (supported, relevant comments): “Identification of writers’ methods. Some reference to subject terminology.”
  • Level 3 (explained, structured comments): “Explained/relevant comments on writer’s methods with some relevant use of subject terminology. Identification of effects of writer’s methods to create meanings.”
  • Level 4 (clear understanding): “Clear explanation of writer’s methods with appropriate use of relevant subject terminology. Understanding of effects of writer’s methods to create meanings.”
Naming “alliteration” with no effect = Level 2. Quote + effect = Level 3. Quote + effect + So What, every time = heading for Level 4.

marking.h: AQA’s indicative content for the extract (things answers might include)
marking.html:
• first vision introducing Scrooge as ‘solitary’
  • description of school as bleak, uncared for place
  • use of cold imagery
  • alliteration of ‘feeble fire’
  • ideas about effect of loneliness and isolation; ideas about the importance of love and compassion
